extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and communicators (PR agencies, government communications officers, in-house comms)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for crafting and distributing timely, targeted press releases that attract media attention or can be repurposed for owned channels. Covers when to use releases, how to pitch, headline and copycraft, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience / pitch selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Send the release to the right audience rather than blasting a broad list of reporters; choose local/regional/state media for government communication and appropriate outlets for the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sending press releases in blast emails to a broad list of reporters almost never works; use that approach sparingly. For government communication, Hamilton County leans into local, regional or state media, which can sometimes lead to broader coverage. Use newswires when wide distribution is the objective (business/financial news in particular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie the release into current events or relevant trends to increase its newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: announcing stormproof windows during a brewing hurricane increases interest. Given the fast modern news cycle and reporters being squeezed for time, releases tied to timely events/trends are more likely to be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling headline and email subject line
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline (and the email subject) is the door-opener and must entice the reader to open the email and read further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doherty often spends as much or more time on the headline and subject line than the body of the release because that's what will grab reporters. Invest time to craft something that will prompt opens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate the who, what, why and when of the news in a concise format; avoid jargon and unnecessary details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a packaged, to-go piece that makes it easy for reporters to use; concise, clear releases increase the likelihood of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / double-check everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure factual accuracy to maintain credibility; avoid mistakes that lead to retractions or corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check all facts, names, dates and figures. There’s nothing worse than having to retract or correct a press release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability for follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ready to follow up and provide additional information or interviews when a reporter or editor calls after a release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you send a release, expect outreach and be prepared to answer questions, provide more assets or set up interviews—being available increases usefulness of the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-alone quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft quotes that can stand alone in a journalist’s article and help tell the brand’s story without requiring long setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of press release quotes as elements that should work independently inside a news story; avoid quotes that need lengthy context to make sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use newswires for wide distribution and SEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswires are the best sources for wide distribution—especially for business and financial news—and can help with SEO even if a release doesn’t generate press interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets like Bloomberg, Reuters and Dow Jones are predisposed to publish company news quickly; posting to a wire can boost discoverability and reach investors and business audiences. Some large online sites (e.g., CNBC, MarketWatch) similarly rely heavily on releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaged-to-go content
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a ready-for-publication package that helps time-pressed reporters file a story quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are squeezed for time; releases that are reliable, current and interesting and packaged for easy use build relationships and increase the likelihood of being noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use cases for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use press releases for major corporate announcements, government operations or countywide initiatives where coverage is likely; softer news may only occasionally elicit response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major announcements such as leadership changes or operations moves at notable companies almost always get some form of coverage. Softer news should be used strategically; it may only get pickup when reporters are in a pinch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass blasts (exception: wires)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid indiscriminately spamming reporters’ inboxes with every update; the one common exception is distributing via newswires for broad reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blast emails to a broad reporter list almost never work; reserve wide blasts for wire distribution when the goal is broad dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurpose non-picked-up releases
rubrics_metrics.description: If a release doesn’t generate media pickup, repurpose the content on the company website or social media to derive value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton County repurposes releases for owned channels; social media buzz can sometimes prompt reporters to call later, so a non-picked-up release is not necessarily wasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know outlet-specific tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Different publications have different reliance on press releases—fast online outlets often publish releases quickly while legacy outlets may be less likely to pick them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets focused on speed (some online business sites) may rely almost exclusively on press releases for initial stories; newspapers like the Wall Street Journal, Financial Times and New York Times are less likely to result in pickup from a release alone.
